What the Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) publishes, how the files are
organised and which release to use. The table lists the other pages.

```{r status}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false
if (v2_current) {
  cat(
    "::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\n",
    "**Current release: ", cfg$release, ".** It covers the days ",
    rel$coverage_text(cfg), ". The previous release, ", cfg$previous_release,
    ", stays available: see [Release ", cfg$previous_release, "](releases.qmd#release-v002).\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat(
    "::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\n",
    "**Release ", cfg$release, " is the upcoming release.** This section describes it. ",
    "Its files are being produced, starting with the days from ",
    rel$day_text(cfg$release_coverage$start), " onwards. Until they are available, use ",
    "release ", cfg$current_release, ", which covers ",
    portal_labels$month_range(cfg$coverage$start, cfg$coverage$end),
    ": see [Release ", cfg$previous_release, "](releases.qmd#release-v002).\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
}
```

## What is published

OPDI starts from the position reports that aircraft broadcast by radio,
received by the [OpenSky Network](https://opensky-network.org/), a network of
ground receivers run by volunteers, universities and other organisations. OPDI
groups the reports of one aircraft into flights and describes each flight in
two ways.

- The **flight list** has one row per flight: the aircraft, call sign,
  departure and destination airports, first and last time seen, and main
  times, such as take-off and landing, and the runways used.
- The **flight events** have one row per event. An **event** is a moment in a
  flight with a time and a position, for example the take-off, the top of
  climb, the crossing of a flight level or the entry into a holding pattern.
  Each row also carries the **measurements** taken at that event, for example
  the distance flown since the start of the flight, and the columns of its
  flight, so one row stands alone.

Columns are listed on the [Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd); how each is
computed is explained in [Algorithms](../algorithms/index.qmd).

## Daily files

Release `r cfg$release` has two files per day:

| File | One row per | Size of one day |
|---|---|---|
| `flight_list/flight_list_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | flight | about 16 MB |
| `flight_events/flight_events_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | event | about 430 MB |

`YYYYMMDD` is the date, for example `20260614`. The sizes were measured on
14 June 2026: 161,881 flights and 6,692,084 events worldwide.

The files are in **Parquet**, a format that stores data by column and that most
tools read: Python (pandas, pyarrow, polars), R (arrow), DuckDB, Spark and
Trino. A program that reads only some columns or rows reads only part of the
file.

Two small files help to find data (columns on the
[Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd#flight-index-and-catalogue)):

- A **flight index** per month, `index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet`: one row
  per flight of the month and the name of the daily file that holds it.
- A **catalogue**, `catalogue.parquet`: one row per published day, with the
  number of flights and events, the time of the first and last event, the file
  sizes and the versions of the methods used.

## Which day a flight belongs to

A flight belongs to the day on which it was **first seen**, in UTC: the column
`dof` (date of flight). The files of a day hold the flights first seen that
day and **all** their events, also those after midnight: a flight that takes
off at 23:30 UTC and lands at 02:00 UTC the next day is in the files of the
day it took off, with its landing.

A few events belong to a track with no row in the flight list (3,338 of
6,691,769 events, or 0.05%, on 14 June 2026). The flight list holds
only tracks for which a departure or a destination airport could be named
(see [Departure and destination airports](../algorithms/airports.qmd)); these
tracks had neither. Their events are published in the file of the day their
track started, with empty flight columns.

## Coverage

Release `r cfg$release` `r if (v2_current) "covers" else "will cover"` the
whole world: every flight that the OpenSky Network received. Release `r cfg$previous_release` covered a box around Europe
only. Reception depends on where receivers are and is thin over the oceans and near
the ground at many airports; see [Limitations](../limitations.qmd#ads-b-reception).
